# Purpose

Differential-analysis results on high-dimensional omics data (gene
expression, microbiome abundance tables) can be driven by a small number of
samples. `looOmics` quantifies this by refitting the model once per
left-out sample and measuring how much the coefficients move.

**This is a sensitivity analysis, not a bad-sample detector.** An
influential sample may reflect genuine biological heterogeneity — a real
subgroup, an extreme but valid responder. Flagged samples should be
inspected, not automatically removed.

The package reruns the relevant pipeline for every leave-one-out fit where
appropriate: for the DESeq2 engine, for example, size factors and
dispersions are re-estimated for every fit.

# Quick start

The recommended interface is a `SummarizedExperiment`. The first example
uses a simulated matrix to introduce the workflow; subsequent examples show
Bioconductor-native inputs.

```{r setup}
library(looOmics)
```

We simulate 200 features, 16 samples, a two-level condition effect on the
first 30 features, and one planted influential sample (S09):

```{r sim}
set.seed(42)
n_feat <- 200
samples <- sprintf("S%02d", 1:16)
condition <- factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = 8))
batch <- factor(rep(c("kit1", "kit2"), times = 8))

assay <- matrix(rnorm(n_feat * 16), n_feat, 16,
                dimnames = list(paste0("g", 1:n_feat), samples))
assay[1:30, condition == "B"] <- assay[1:30, condition == "B"] + 1.2

# planted influential sample: S09 (group B) has extreme values on g1-g20
assay[1:20, "S09"] <- assay[1:20, "S09"] + 6

col_data <- data.frame(
    condition = condition, batch = batch,
    depth = round(rnorm(16, mean = 5e6, sd = 4e5)),
    extraction = factor(rep(c("good", "good", "good", "bad"), times = 4)),
    row.names = samples
)
```

## Run the leave-one-out analysis

```{r loo}
res <- loo_sensitivity(assay, ~ condition + batch, col_data = col_data)
res
```

## Bioconductor input interoperability

`looOmics` uses `SummarizedExperiment` as its primary Bioconductor input
interface. The assay stores features in rows and samples in columns, while
`colData` stores the biological and technical sample metadata used both in
the differential model and in downstream influence profiling.

```{r summarized-experiment}
se <- SummarizedExperiment::SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(logcounts = assay),
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(col_data)
)
res_se <- loo_sensitivity(
    se, ~ condition + batch, engine = "lm",
    assay_name = "logcounts", parallel = FALSE
)
res_se
```

For count-based RNA-seq analyses, use raw non-negative integer counts with
the DESeq2 engine. The engine reconstructs and refits the DESeq2 workflow for
each omitted sample, re-estimating size factors and dispersions rather than
rounding or reusing normalized values.

```{r deseq2-summarized-experiment}
set.seed(21)
count_samples <- sprintf("C%02d", 1:12)
count_condition <- factor(rep(c("control", "treated"), each = 6),
                          levels = c("control", "treated"))
count_meta <- data.frame(condition = count_condition,
                         row.names = count_samples)
count_matrix <- matrix(
    rnbinom(100 * 12, mu = 100, size = 10), nrow = 100,
    dimnames = list(paste0("gene", 1:100), count_samples)
)
count_matrix[1:20, count_condition == "treated"] <-
    count_matrix[1:20, count_condition == "treated"] + 80L
se_counts <- SummarizedExperiment::SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(counts = count_matrix),
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(count_meta)
)
res_deseq2 <- loo_sensitivity(
    se_counts, ~ condition, engine = "deseq2",
    assay_name = "counts", parallel = FALSE, fitType = "mean"
)
res_deseq2
```

The `shifts` table records, for every feature, model term, and left-out
sample, the full-sample coefficient, the LOO coefficient, the raw shift
(`delta`), the standardized deletion shift (`dfbetas`), full and LOO p-values,
BH-adjusted q-values, within-term feature ranks, rank changes, and whether the
feature's significance status flipped. A positive `rank_change` means the
feature moved to a numerically larger (weaker) rank after sample deletion:

```{r shifts}
head(tidy(res, what = "shifts"))
```

For ordinary linear models `dfbetas` coincides with classical DFBETAS; for
other engines it is the analogous deletion-based standardized shift.

## Flag influential samples

```{r flag}
res <- flag_influential(res, method = "topk", k = 2)
res
```

The planted sample S09 is recovered as the most influential sample:

```{r topflags}
flags <- tidy(res, what = "flags")
flags[order(-flags$score), ]
```

Per-term influence scores show which model terms drive each sample's
score:

```{r byterm}
head(influence_by_term(res))
```

## Profile flags against metadata

```{r profile}
res <- profile_flags(res, model_covariates = c("condition", "batch"))
profiles(res)
```

The profile evaluates associations between flagged status and all selected
sample metadata, including the original model variables (`condition` and
`batch`) as well as technical variables (`depth` and `extraction`). In-model
variables are explicitly labeled. P-values are BH-adjusted across the
univariate family; an adjusted logistic model is fit only when the sample size
and design support it. Covariates that cannot be tested are reported with
reasons rather than silently dropped.

## Plot

```{r plot, fig.alt = "Bar plot of per-sample influence scores; the planted sample S09 stands out."}
plot(res)
```

# Relationship to existing Bioconductor tools

`limma` and `DESeq2` provide established differential-expression modeling
frameworks (Ritchie et al., 2015; Love et al., 2014). `looOmics` does not
replace either package: it repeatedly refits these engines after omitting one
sample at a time, then compares coefficients, standard errors, adjusted
p-values, and within-term feature rankings. It also connects sample influence
to biological and technical metadata. This provides an additional
sensitivity-analysis layer around existing differential-analysis workflows.

For limma, users should supply appropriately normalized and log-transformed
expression values. For DESeq2, users should supply raw integer counts. The
package deliberately does not silently convert normalized or transformed
values into counts.

# Parallel execution

`looOmics` never changes the `future` plan itself; users control it:

```{r parallel, eval = FALSE}
future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 4)
res <- loo_sensitivity(se, ~ condition + batch, engine = "lm")
future::plan(future::sequential)
```

- Ritchie, M. E., Phipson, B., Wu, D., Hu, Y., Law, C. W., Shi, W., and
